 Pressure Gauge Accuracy Classes Explained: 8 Reliable ASME B40.100 Grades to Avoid Costly Mistakes

 Two gauges can look identical on the shelf and still disagree by 5% of span at the same reading, purely because they carry different ASME accuracy grades. Knowing what those grade letters actually mean is what keeps a spec sheet honest.

 4A to D Explained 
 




 Pressure gauge accuracy classes under ASME B40.100 define exactly how much error a gauge is allowed, as a percent of its full span, so engineers can compare gauges from different manufacturers on equal terms.


 Every dial pressure gauge sold for industrial use carries an accuracy grade somewhere on its dial or datasheet, usually written as a letter and number like 2A, 1A, or B. That grade isn't a marketing label. It's a defined tolerance from ASME B40.100 , the American standard that governs dial and digital pressure gauges, and it tells you precisely how far a reading is allowed to drift from the true pressure.


 
 
 

 Get the accuracy class wrong on a specification and one of two things happens. Either the plant pays for a far more precise gauge than the process ever needed, or a critical measurement ends up relying on a gauge that was never built to hold the tolerance the application actually requires. Both mistakes are avoidable once the eight ASME B40.100 grades are actually understood.

 Quick Answer
 What Are Pressure Gauge Accuracy Classes?
 Pressure gauge accuracy classes under ASME B40.100 define the permissible error as a percent of span, from Grade 4A (±0.1%) through 3A (±0.25%), 2A (±0.5%) and 1A (±1.0%) to Grade A (2 to 1 to 2%) and looser grades.
 Formula: Allowable Error = (Grade % / 100) × Full Scale Span . Example: a Grade 2A gauge with a 0 to 300 psi range has an allowable error of (0.5 / 100) × 300 = 1.5 psi at any point on the dial.

 Why Pressure Gauge Accuracy Classes Exist

 Before ASME formalized these grades, two manufacturers could both call a gauge "accurate" while meaning completely different things by it. One might be quoting error at mid scale only, another might be quoting the worst case anywhere on the dial, and a buyer had no simple way to compare them side by side.

 ASME B40.100 fixes that by forcing every accuracy claim into one of eight standardized boxes. Once a gauge is stamped Grade 2A, that number means exactly the same thing whether the gauge came from a large multinational manufacturer or a small regional shop, because both were tested against the same permissible error table.

 This matters most during calibration and audits. An instrument technician checking a gauge against a certified reference standard needs to know the pass or fail tolerance before running the test, and the accuracy grade printed on the dial is exactly that tolerance, already defined
